the synthesis of leukaemiainhibitory factor (L1F) in normal or diseased human kidney fragments, in vitro.
LIF synthesis by normal and diseased human kidneys and its regulation in vitro and in renal transplant recipients.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the LIF production in kidney is regulated by inflammatory mediators and that it is increased in renal inflammatory diseases, but that it does not appear to be involved in acute renal rejection.
LIF production by renal fragments in vitro and in renal transplants in vivo is enhanced by IL-1beta, and inhibited by IL4 and dexamethasome, except in two episodes of severe rejection.
LIF production by diseased kidneys is enhanced compared to normal kidneys, and is modulated by pro- and anti- inflammatory stimuli.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
LIF is a pleiotrophic cytokine which is produced by the kidney and by the renal cells.
LIF production is enhanced in inflammatory kidney diseases, but the response of LIF to pro- and inflammatory stimuli may be delayed in renal transplanted kidneys.
LIF production is enhanced by inflammatory stimuli and is involved in the pathophysiology of kidney diseases.
The main takeaway from our work is that

leukaemia inhibiting factor (LIF): 1) is a pleotrophic cytokine involved in nephrogenic processes; 2) is released by the kidney itself in response to local inflammatory stimuli; 3) is produced by human renal cells (mesangial cells, renal tubular epithelium cells) as well as by diseased kidneys; 4) is enhanced by proinflammatory cytokines and inhibited by dexamethasome or IL-4.
LIF is produced by the diseased kidney itself, and that it can be regulated by inflammatory mediators.
LIF production by kidney cells can be modulated by inflammatory cytokines, and that LIF production is enhanced in diseased kidneys.
